This dataset contains dialogue from three of Shakespeare's most recognized works: Hamlet, Macbeth, and Romeo and Juliet. I will only be working with Romeo and Juiliet, which was one of my favorite high school readings.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

romeo_juliet <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/romeo_juliet.csv')

love_rates <- romeo_juliet |> 
    filter(character != "[stage direction]") |>
    mutate(randj_vs_everybodyelse = if_else(character == "Romeo" | character == "Juliet", "Romeo and Juliet", "Everyone else")) |>
    mutate(love_count = str_count(dialogue, "(?i)\\blove\\b")) |>
    group_by(randj_vs_everybodyelse) |>
    summarize(total_love = sum(love_count), total_lines = n()) |>
    mutate(love_rate = (total_love/total_lines)*100) |>
    mutate(randj_vs_everybodyelse = fct_reorder(randj_vs_everybodyelse, love_rate, .desc = TRUE))

ggplot(love_rates, aes(x = randj_vs_everybodyelse, y = love_rate, fill = randj_vs_everybodyelse)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(title = "Comparison of 'Love' Rates in Romeo and Juliet", y = "'Love' per 100 lines", x = NULL, fill = "Romeo and Juliet vs. All Other Characters")

```

This column chart shows that the rate of the word 'Love' (case insensitive, including the possessive 'love's' but excluding words like loved, lovely, beloved, etc.), calculated as (total count of 'Love' / total lines spoken by the group * 100) is more than twice as high for the two title characters when compared with all other characters combined in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet. The characters Romeo and Juliet have a love rate of about 7.5 per 100 lines, while the other characters' love rate is about 3.3 per 100 lines. The data doesn't show who is talking to whom, just the speaker groups' love rates.

```{r}
words_before_love <- romeo_juliet |> 
    filter(character != "[stage direction]") |>
    mutate(randj_vs_everybodyelse = if_else(character == "Romeo" | character == "Juliet", "Romeo and Juliet", "Everyone else")) |>
    filter(str_detect(dialogue, "(?i)\\blove\\b")) |>
    mutate(word_before_love = str_to_lower(str_extract(dialogue, "(?i)\\b\\w+(?= love\\b)"))) |>
    filter(!is.na(word_before_love)) |>
    filter(str_detect(word_before_love, "^(my|thy|your)$"))

ggplot(words_before_love, aes(x = word_before_love, fill = randj_vs_everybodyelse)) +
    geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
    labs(y = "Number of lines", x = NULL, title = "Distribution of Words That Precede 'Love' in Romeo and Juliet", fill = "Romeo and Juliet vs. All Other Characters")

```

This bar chart compares the distribution of three possessive words in the dialogue that precede 'Love' (case insensitive). I used a lookahead to capture the word before 'love' or 'love's' in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet. The two title characters say 'my' before 'love' much more often than all of the other characters combined (8 times vs. 1), whereas 'thy' precedes love for all other characters one more time than for the two title characters (5 times vs. 4). 'Your' comes before love one more time for all of the other characters (2 vs. 1). There are only 21 total lines where my, thy, or your precede love, out of 123 total lines with a word before love; it is quite small. The gaps between character groups for the possessives 'thy' and 'your' are only one instance, so it doesn't tell us much about the use of the possessives across the two groups. Romeo and Juliet are the main lovers in the play, and speak about their own feelings of love frequently, which likely explains why 'my' precedes the word 'love' more for the two title characters.
